evidence_quotes.quote: Este artículo manifiesta la necesidad de una nueva Ley de Aguas que reconozca y operativice el derecho humano al agua potable y saneamiento, ordenando la institucionalidad y creando mecanismos para garantizar la disponibilidad, cantidad, calidad y accesibilidad del agua.

En este artículo se profundiza la discusión planteada en dicha ponencia, a partir de una exploración documental tendiente a caracterizar la acción institucional y los marcos normativos relacionados con la gestión del agua en Costa Rica y su garantía como un derecho humano. Se revisó literatura relacionada con el contexto legal e institucional de la gestión y derecho humano al agua, protestas ambientales y casos particulares de conflictos por el agua, asimismo se consultó con expertos y expertas en el tema.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3 (Contexto institucional y legal para el agua en Costa Rica)
evidence_quotes.quote: La gestión del agua en Costa Rica ocurre entonces en un entorno institucional centralizado que se caracteriza por el traslape de competencias, bajo un marco legal complejo de operativizar y que debido a su antigüedad no incorpora de forma explícita criterios ni mecanismos efectivos para atender realidades como la crisis climática o la intensificación de actividades extractivas.

En este sentido, la amplia cobertura domiciliar del servicio público de agua potable en el país contrasta con el hecho de que el suministro se interrumpe en muchas comunidades durante varias horas al día por la escasez del recurso, especialmente durante los meses de menos lluvia cuando también disminuye el caudal de ríos y fuentes subterráneas.

criterion_notes.c1: Discusses household and community access to drinking water and sanitation services in Costa Rica (including national household coverage, rural community aqueducts/ASADAS, intermittent supply, and pesticide contamination of community water systems), alongside broader water-resource conflicts.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this paper passes (yes): it discusses legal, institutional, and regulatory factors in Costa Rica, including the 1942 Water Law No. 276, overlapping competencies across 13 institutions (ICAA, MINAE, SENARA), Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV) jurisprudence on the human right to water, and stalled legislative Water Law bills. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it is unclear/borderline (leaning no): the paper primarily frames macro-governance institutional fragmentation, failed IWRM legislative reform, and normative human-rights arguments rather than analyzing a specific rule-type mechanism governing household service access, although it descriptively mentions Sala IV Vote 2002-10766 (barring total disconnection without an alternative source), ASADA delegation, and weak regulatory enforcement/concession oversight. Regardless of whether the plain or narrow reading of Criterion 2 is applied, the paper is excluded under E05 for lack of empirical evidence.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (exclude as E05). This is a narrative documentary policy overview and normative human-rights essay, not an empirical study or systematic synthesis. Although the Methodology section mentions a prior 2014-2016 research project in La Cruz and states in passing that experts were consulted, it reports zero primary data, no interview sample or protocol, no qualitative or quantitative empirical analysis, and no systematic review methodology, relying instead on secondary national reports (Estado de la Nación, UN Special Rapporteur), court rulings, and news articles.
criterion_notes.c4: Mentions secondary national statistics (93.9% drinking-water coverage, 14.4% wastewater treatment) and secondary legal/media accounts of rural aqueduct contamination with bromacil and daily service interruptions, but reports no primary empirical or systematically synthesized access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not provide an identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample/unit of analysis, or operationalized exposure-outcome analysis because it is a narrative documentary and normative commentary.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in Spanish (with Spanish and English abstracts). Per Criterion 10, direct assessment and translation from the provided Spanish full text is feasible; however, the study is ineligible on empirical grounds (E05).

study_design: Narrative documentary and policy overview / normative human-rights commentary (non-empirical)
exposure: Institutional fragmentation and regulatory ambiguity in Costa Rican water governance (1942 Water Law No. 276, overlapping institutional competencies, failed legislative reforms, and weak environmental/concession enforcement)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Full text (8 pages, in Spanish) matches the record metadata. Although the paper discusses drinking-water and sanitation access and institutional/regulatory ambiguity in Costa Rica, it is a narrative documentary overview and normative human-rights policy essay advocating for a new Water Law rather than an empirical study or systematic synthesis. In the Methodology section, the authors note that the article builds on an earlier conference presentation via an unsystematic documentary exploration, literature review, and unspecified expert consultation, but no primary empirical data, participant sample, interview methods, or systematic synthesis are presented; the body text summarizes secondary national reports, legislative bills, court rulings, and media accounts of socio-environmental water conflicts. Exclusion holds under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.
